questions.question: Describe the audit method for household plastics and list the long-life plastics built into a modern house with the reason each replaced an older material.
questions.expected_answer: The audit goes room by room listing every plastic item, identifying the plastic from its recycling code, feel and use, noting the property that chose it and estimating its lifespan, then sorting the items into built-in, durable and packaging groups. Built-in plastics include PVC water and waste pipes, which replaced galvanised steel and cast iron because they do not corrode or fur up, are light, cheap and join with solvent cement; PVC conduit and cable sheath for insulation; uPVC window frames, rigid and weather-proof and never needing paint; polystyrene ceiling insulation; polyethylene damp-proof sheeting; and a rotationally moulded UV-stabilised polyethylene roof tank. These made housing cheaper to build and longer lasting, with the trade-off that PVC releases chlorine gas in a fire and foam insulation must be behind fire-resistant board.

questions.question: For the kitchen and bathroom, name the plastic used for at least six items and state the property that chose each.
questions.expected_answer: Kettle body and handle: polypropylene, tough, cheap and able to take boiling water, with the handle insulating against heat. Fridge inner liner: ABS or HIPS, easy to clean and not cracking in the cold, with polyurethane foam insulation in the walls. Chopping board: HDPE, which does not absorb water and can be bleached. Microwave containers: polypropylene, which holds its shape above 100 degrees. Children's plates: melamine, a thermoset that resists heat and scratches. Cooldrink bottles: PET, clear and strong; milk bottles: HDPE. Bath: glass-fibre reinforced acrylic, warm, light and moulded in one piece. Toothbrush: polypropylene handle with nylon bristles, which are strong and wear-resistant. Buckets and laundry baskets: polypropylene or HDPE, tough and water-resistant.

questions.question: Explain the three lifespan groups of household plastics with their end-of-life routes, and give four safety rules for plastics in the home.
questions.expected_answer: Built-in services such as pipes and frames last forty years or more and end as rubble when the house is demolished, though uPVC frames and pipes are increasingly recycled; durable goods such as kettles, chairs and buckets last two to twenty years and, being mostly single-polymer, can be recycled if they reach a collector; packaging lasts minutes to days, is the most numerous group and is where reduce and reuse matter most, since only clean PET, HDPE and some polypropylene and LDPE are recycled. Safety rules: heat food only in plastics marked microwave-safe, such as polypropylene, not polystyrene, melamine or PVC; keep plastics out of prolonged sunlight and away from stoves, since heat and UV weaken them; keep small loose parts away from infants, who can choke on them; and because plastic furniture, foam and PVC burn with dense toxic smoke, use flame-retarded foam and fit a smoke alarm.
